Ability means the power to do something. It is the answer to the question: "Can this person actually do this thing?"

When someone has the ability to do something, it means they possess what it takes — the mental power, the physical capacity, the skill, or the knowledge — to actually carry it out.

A bird has the ability to fly. A fish does not.
She has the ability to solve complex math problems.
He lost the ability to walk after his accident.

Notice that "ability" is about what is possible for someone — what lies within their reach.

Ability can come from two sources, and this matters:

1. Natural ability — something you are born with. Some people are naturally gifted at music, athletics, or learning languages. They didn't earn it through hard work; they simply have it. This is sometimes called a natural talent, but the word "ability" covers it perfectly.

She showed a natural ability for drawing even as a child.

2. Acquired (or developed) ability — something you gain through practice, education, or experience. Most abilities in life fall here. You weren't born knowing how to drive a car or write code — you learned it, and now you can do it.

After years of training, he had the ability to speak four languages.

In everyday use, "ability" covers both kinds without needing to specify which one, unless you want to.

Having the "ability" to do something doesn't mean doing it perfectly. It simply means you can do it — but the level at which you can do it varies widely.

Think of it as a scale:

  • At the low end: You barely manage it. You can do it, but with difficulty.
  • In the middle: You do it competently and reliably.
  • At the high end: You do it with exceptional skill and ease.

This is why you'll often see ability described with words like great, limited, remarkable, poor, or extraordinary — because ability comes in degrees.

He has limited ability in swimming — he can stay afloat, but only just.
She has remarkable ability as a surgeon.
Ability Can Be General or Specific

General ability refers to broad mental or physical capacity — the overall potential a person has.

He is a person of great ability. (meaning: he is broadly capable and intelligent)

Specific ability refers to being able to do one particular thing.

She has the ability to memorize long texts quickly.
The machine has the ability to process 10,000 records per second.

Both uses are equally correct. Context makes clear which one is meant.

These words are close cousins, but each has a slightly different shade of meaning:

Skill — Skill is always something learned and practiced. It implies that you have refined a specific ability through deliberate effort and repetition. All skills are abilities, but not all abilities are skills.

Playing the piano is a skill. (It had to be learned.)
A child's natural ability to absorb language is not yet a skill.

Talent — Talent specifically refers to a natural, inborn ability. It implies something you were gifted with, not something you worked hard to get. "Ability" is the broader, more neutral word; "talent" emphasizes the natural origin.

She has a talent for music. (She was born with it.)
She has the ability to play the violin. (This is what she can do — however she got there.)

Capability — Very close to ability, but capability often suggests the outer limit of what someone could do under the right conditions. It leans toward potential.

The engine has the capability to reach 200 mph. (Under the right conditions, it can.)
Ability tends to describe what someone actually does or regularly can do, while capability often speaks to what they could do if pushed.

Capacity — Capacity usually refers to the maximum amount something can hold or handle, or the potential to develop a skill or quality. It often sounds more abstract or physiological.

The human brain has a remarkable capacity for learning.
Ability is more about concrete, actual doing; capacity is more about room or potential.

The short rule: when in doubt, use ability — it is the most versatile of all these words.

Here are the most natural ways "ability" is used in sentences, all of which you will encounter repeatedly:

  • "the ability to [do something]" — the most standard structure.

He has the ability to remain calm under pressure.

  • "to the best of one's ability" — meaning as well as one possibly can, using every bit of what they have.

She completed the task to the best of her ability.

  • "of great/limited/exceptional ability" — describing how able someone is overall.

He is a student of great ability.

  • "natural ability" — something one was born with.

Her natural ability made her stand out immediately.

  • "mixed abilities" — used in education to describe groups where learners have different levels of competence.

The teacher was skilled at handling mixed-ability classrooms.

  • "mental/physical/intellectual ability" — specifying what type of ability is being discussed.

The test was designed to measure mental ability.
One Important Distinction: Ability vs. Opportunity

"Ability" is only about what a person can do — their internal power. It says nothing about whether they are allowed to do it or get the chance to do it.

She has the ability to lead a team, but her company never gave her the opportunity.

This is a meaningful distinction in life: a person may have great ability but lack access, opportunity, or permission. "Ability" only covers their side of the equation.
Ability is the power or capacity — whether natural or learned — that a person or thing has to perform an action or achieve a result, and it comes in varying degrees from very little to exceptional.
